title: My boss gave us a rule down to the SECOND. I followed it. #shorts

lines: My manager said I had to stay on calls until four p.m. and one second. So I hung up at that exact moment.
I worked on an IT help desk at a hospital.
Every shift started with logging into seven different programs. That took ten to fifteen minutes.
Then the manager sent us an email.
We had to be ready for calls one second before the shift started, and stay on the phone until one second after it ended.
So I followed that email. For a while.
Then a call came in with less than two minutes left on my shift.
I answered, took the caller's name and location, and listened as they began describing the problem.
The clock hit four p.m. and one second.
I apologized, said my shift was over, ended the call, logged off, and went home.
The caller complained. My manager called me into his office.
He said I should have finished the call.
I showed him the email he'd sent us.
It said I could log off one second after my shift ended.
And that was exactly what I had done.
Did it help my career? Probably not. But it was his rule.
fact_check_notes: Original shift example: 7:00 a.m.–4:00 p.m., ready at 6:59:59, permitted to log off after 4:00:01.
Seven software programs took approximately 10–15 minutes to start and sign into.
Call arrived less than two minutes before the shift end; narrator got caller's name/location and heard part of their issue.
Narrator hung up at shift end, complaint to manager, meeting, cited manager's email.
Author described the act as career-limiting; no firing, policy reversal, apology, or lawsuit claimed.
editorial_notes: Pronounce 4:00:01 as 'four p.m. and one second' for clarity. Opening line may be tightened in the final voice pass.
